nameStory: The Greylag Goose gets its name from being a 'grey lag' — meaning it was the grey goose that lagged behind when other geese migrated south for winter. Many Greylag populations stay put year-round rather than migrating, earning them this 'slowpoke' reputation among waterfowl watchers.
description: The Greylag Goose is a hefty waterbird that looks like the classic farm goose — and that's no coincidence, since it's the ancestor of most domestic geese! These large birds measure about 3 feet long and weigh around 7 pounds, with beautiful mottled grey and white feathers that create a barred pattern across their bodies. You'll recognize them by their bright orange beaks and pink legs, which stand out against their more subdued plumage. While not native to New England, small numbers show up here, likely escapees from farms or parks that have gone wild.

idTips.label: Orange Beak
idTips.description: The thick, bright orange bill is unmistakable and feels sturdy if you ever handle one — much more substantial than a duck's bill and completely orange without dark markings

idTips.label: Pink Legs
idTips.description: Stout pink or pinkish-orange legs that look robust enough to support this hefty bird — they feel warm and slightly rough to the touch

idTips.label: Mottled Grey Plumage
idTips.description: Feathers have a beautiful barred and mottled pattern of grey and white that feels soft and dense, creating an overall greyish appearance from a distance

idTips.label: Large Size
idTips.description: Noticeably bigger than most ducks and comparable to Canada Geese — you'd need both hands to hold one, and they have a substantial, meaty feel

idTips.label: Honking Call
idTips.description: Makes loud, resonant honking sounds similar to domestic geese — the kind of honk you'd hear on a farm that carries well across water

habitat: In New England, Greylag Geese are most likely found around ponds, lakes, and marshy areas in parks, golf courses, or suburban settings where they've established small resident populations. They prefer areas with both water access and nearby grassy fields for feeding, often showing up at the same spots year after year. Look for them in places where domestic waterfowl are kept, as some populations started from farm escapees.

seasonality.spring: Breeding season brings more vocal behavior and you might spot pairs with goslings in tow. Adults will be very protective of young and may approach aggressively if you get too close.
seasonality.summer: Family groups stay together, with fuzzy grey goslings gradually developing adult plumage. This is when they're most likely to be seen grazing on grass in open areas near water.
seasonality.fall: While many goose species migrate through, Greylag Geese often stay put in established territories. You may see them joining mixed flocks of other geese species.
seasonality.winter: Most visible during this season as they gather in open water that hasn't frozen and continue grazing on available grass and waste grain in fields.

funFact: Every Thanksgiving turkey dinner has an unlikely connection to Greylag Geese — these birds were domesticated over 3,000 years ago and became so important that ancient Egyptians used geese as currency, literally paying taxes with them!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with large domestic geese, which makes sense since farm geese are their descendants. Wild Greylags tend to be more wary of humans and have slightly more refined features, while domestic geese are often chunkier and more approachable. Remember: if it acts like a farm goose but seems skittish, it might be a wild Greylag.
contextualKnowledge: In North America, the name is often spelled 'Graylag' rather than 'Greylag,' but they're the same species. Most Greylag Geese in New England are likely either escapees from captivity or their descendants, rather than true wild migrants, so they represent an interesting case of semi-feral populations establishing themselves in new areas.
compareHints: Among the grey geese in its genus, Greylag Geese lack the white forehead patch of Greater White-fronted Geese and aren't pure white like Snow Geese. They're larger and more robust than Pink-footed Geese, with that distinctive all-orange bill rather than a pink and black one. Think of them as the 'plain' grey goose — no fancy markings, just solid grey and white with bright orange accessories.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the Greater White-fronted Goose which has a white forehead patch and orange legs, Snow Geese are predominantly white all over with black wingtips.
Unlike Snow Geese which are mostly white or very pale, Greater White-fronted Geese are brown and gray with distinctive belly markings.
Among the grey geese, Pink-footed Geese are smaller and more compact than Greylag Geese, lack the white forehead of Greater White-fronted Geese, and have much pinker legs than any of their relatives.
Compared to Snow Geese in the same genus, Ross's Geese are significantly smaller with proportionally smaller, cleaner bills lacking black edges.
Among grey geese, Swan Goose is unmistakable due to its exceptionally long neck and orange bill.
Compared to other grey geese in its genus, Tundra Bean Goose lacks the white forehead patch of Greater White-fronted Goose and the distinctive bill pattern of Pink-footed Goose.
